editorial.text: A library visitor once complimented me by saying that my library did not have the “stench of death”. He meant that the library’s appearance showed that the place was still valued. There was no damage outside or graffiti and interior was warm and welcoming with up to date displays and very little fossilised blue-tack on the walls. The thing is, though, I know libraries with that smell. I have been to libraries where the council, not mine thank goodness, clearly does not care and, sadly, the library teams have been unable to keep up their morale. This lethal infection starts from the head: if the council does not invest in its libraries then sooner or later – and it can take decades – the local library starts looking awful. And people don’t come in, and the vicious circle of decline in investment and in usage becomes evident. But this does not need to be the case. A well-maintained and attractive building, with money enough to change with the times, will lead to a thriving library. But where does the money come from? Well, ultimately, from central government, either through direct grant or through sufficiently funding councils. And this has not happened sufficiently in decades, Since the start of this website in 2010, we have had a decade of austerity – where the already-insufficient funding in infrastructure has been cut – followed by years where funding has been stable but has not taken into account inflation or the demands of social welfare. Many of us were excited when a new party came to power, but it quickly became apparent under Starmer that nothing would change. And now there is renewed hope for the new prime minister, but the budget this week showed a slight change in the mood music at least. A good a time in a decade or two to ask for money then. But in order to do this, we need to know how much we want, so the new Arup and Designing Libraries Collaboration is to be welcomed. This will “establish the first comprehensive assessment of library capital investment requirements in almost two decades.” It’s been done before – the 2006 report identified £760 million was needed – but then in 2010 it all became moot when the Government made clear none of it was going to happen. But that was 20 years ago. A recent similar project Evaluating Capital Investment Needs for Arts Centres in the UK was quoted in this year’s Hodge Review and may have influenced Lisa Nandy. So how will it work? Inevitably, it’s all voluntary. Individual councils will be asked for what is needed and it is to be hoped that they will answer honestly and that they will see it’s in their best interest to do so. And if some councils don’t get involved because the figure is too embarrassing for them … well, at least we will know where the smell is coming from.
